failure_modes: False-positive identity calls: Non-vesicular complexes (protein aggregates, lipoproteins, other secretome components) that survive detergent/protease treatment or bind capture reagents produce capture-positive, particle-coincident signals indistinguishable from bona fide EVs under the proposed detergent/protease conditions (assay-level false acceptance).

Spike-in non-equivalence: The exogenous intact-EV spike-in tracer does not reproduce the mechanical, chemical, or surface-epitope vulnerability of endogenous EV subpopulations during device/formulation passage, so spike-in recovery validates only the spike-in behavior and can mask endogenous loss of phenotype (misleading internal control).

Assay interference / false negatives: Formulation excipients or device rinse residues interfere with immuno-capture (blocking, crosslinking, or altering antigen accessibility) causing loss of capture-signal that is assay-artifactual rather than reflecting true membrane damage (false rejection of acceptable EVs).

Co-elution confounds: Fractionation methods (SEC, cushion/iodixanol) permit co-elution of small particles or soluble complexes with similar size/density to EVs, so particle-peak co-localization with capture-signal can arise from non-EV species; detergent/protease conditions may not degrade some structured non-vesicular complexes, producing persistent signal.

Insufficient analytical sensitivity or dynamic range: Low endogenous EV abundance after device/formulation passage (or strong nasal retention/clearance in larger species) yields signal near background, making qualitative pass/fail calls unmeasurable or highly variable across lots.

Inter-lot and inter-source variability: Biological lot-to-lot heterogeneity in surface-epitope display means the chosen multi-epitope panel may only detect a subset of biologically relevant EVs, reducing reproducibility and leading to inconsistent pass/fail outcomes across ≥3 lots.

Species and delivery-route mismatch: Large-animal intranasal biodistribution (strong nasal retention, negligible brain uptake) suggests device/formulation stresses and host mucosal interactions differ across species; an in vitro device-passage identity gate may not predict in vivo delivery or relevance to human intranasal administration.

Operational assay limits: Detergent/protease+RNase conditions and capture formats may need extensive optimization; suboptimal selection could either remove true EV signal (overly harsh) or leave non-vesicular survivors (insufficient), and the proposal lacks a defined orthogonal orthogonal biochemical degradation (e.g., lipid-specific hydrolysis) to adjudicate such cases.
strongest_objection: The single strongest bounded failure mode is that assay-positive, detergent-resistant capture signal after device/formulation passage will not reliably report bona fide membrane-protected EVs but instead reflect either (A) non-vesicular, detergent/protease-resistant complexes that bind the chosen capture reagents or (B) assay interference by formulation/device residues — and these alternatives cannot be excluded by the proposed workflow because (1) spike-in tracers may not faithfully mimic endogenous EVs across device/formulation stresses or co-elution behavior, and (2) co-fractionation of aggregates/protein complexes (and species- or device-dependent retention shown in large-animal intranasal work) can produce qualitatively similar readouts even when endogenous EV identity or in vivo delivery competence is lost.
